# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils in the myocardium, leading to progressive ventricular wall thickening, diastolic dysfunction, and ultimately heart failure and conduction disease [1]. Two types of precursor protein are responsible for most cardiac amyloidosis cases: transthyretin amyloid, and immunoglobulin-derived light chain amyloid. Together these account for the overwhelming majority of cases, and the majority of cases (>98%) are related to monoclonal immunoglobulin light chain (AL) or transthyretin (ATTR) deposition [2]. Once considered rare and untreatable, CA has been transformed over the past decade by advances in noninvasive diagnosis and the emergence of effective disease-modifying therapy [3].

## Pathophysiology

Transthyretin (TTR), formerly known as prealbumin, is a tetrameric carrier protein for thyroxine and retinol-binding protein, synthesized predominantly by the liver [4]. Through gene mutation or aging of the protein, TTR can become unstable and break up into oligomers, which aggregate into insoluble fibrils called TTR amyloid that deposit into extracellular space or tissues. ATTR amyloidosis occurs in two forms: a hereditary (variant) form caused by pathogenic TTR mutations, and a wild-type form associated with aging [5]. In the hereditary subtype, the specific site of an amino acid substitution determines the phenotype of the disease, which is transmitted as autosomal dominant with high penetrance, with clinical manifestations occurring most commonly after the age of 40. In AL amyloidosis, a clonal plasma-cell disorder produces misfolded immunoglobulin light chains that deposit in the heart and kidneys, conferring a particularly poor prognosis when cardiac involvement is advanced [6].

## Epidemiology

ATTR-CA has been increasingly recognized as a cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) in older adults [1]. In a landmark prospective study, wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis is an underdiagnosed cause of HFpEF, and investigators sought to determine its prevalence among elderly patients admitted due to HFpEF; remarkably, ATTRwt accounts for a significant number (13%) of HFpEF cases [7]. Wild-type ATTR predominantly affects men over 70 years of age, whereas variant ATTR phenotypes vary with the underlying mutation [5].

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

Diagnosis is frequently delayed because of nonspecific symptoms and overlap with other causes of left ventricular hypertrophy [8]. A high index of suspicion is warranted in older patients with HFpEF, concentric "hypertrophy," carpal tunnel syndrome, or discordance between voltage and wall thickness on electrocardiography [9]. Echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance with extracellular volume mapping are valuable, but the major breakthrough came with bone scintigraphy. Cardiac transthyretin amyloidosis diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed because of the limited specificity of echocardiography and the traditional requirement for histological confirmation; technetium-labeled bone scintigraphy tracers can localize to myocardial amyloid deposits. In a pivotal multicenter study, the bone-seeking radionuclide tracers 99mTc-DPD, 99mTc-HMDP, and 99mTc-pyrophosphate have high sensitivity for cardiac transthyretin deposits and can differentiate immunoglobulin light chain amyloidosis [10]. Importantly, the diagnostic algorithm requires concurrent exclusion of a monoclonal protein by serum and urine testing; multimodality imaging consensus recommendations have standardized this approach [11]. Professional society statements from the American Heart Association and the European Society of Cardiology now provide structured guidance for evaluation and management [12,13].

## Treatment of ATTR Cardiomyopathy

The therapeutic landscape has been revolutionized by agents targeting different steps of amyloidogenesis [14]. TTR stabilizers prevent tetramer dissociation, the rate-limiting step in fibril formation. In the pivotal ATTR-ACT trial, 441 patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy were randomly assigned in a 2:1:2 ratio to receive 80 mg of tafamidis, 20 mg of tafamidis, or placebo for 30 months [15]. ATTR-ACT showed that tafamidis is the first treatment to improve survival and quality of life in ATTR-CM, with reductions in all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations [16]. A long-term extension confirmed a sustained survival benefit [17].

A next-generation stabilizer, acoramidis, was subsequently evaluated. Efficacy and safety of acoramidis in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy was reported in 2024, demonstrating significant benefit on the primary composite end point [18]; acoramidis showed statistically significant reductions in the composite of all-cause mortality or first cardiovascular-related hospitalization evident within 3 months and sustained through 30 months [19].

Gene-silencing therapies reduce hepatic TTR production. In the APOLLO-B trial, patients with hereditary or wild-type ATTR cardiac amyloidosis were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive patisiran or placebo once every 3 weeks for 12 months [20]; treatment with patisiran preserved functional capacity, health status, and quality of life over 12 months [20]. The subcutaneous small-interfering RNA vutrisiran provided more definitive outcome data in HELIOS-B [21]. Vutrisiran in patients with transthyretin amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy was reported, with results published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2025, and vutrisiran was approved in 2025 by the FDA and EMA for ATTR-CM [22]. Emerging approaches include in vivo gene editing: at day 28, the mean reduction from baseline in serum TTR protein concentration was 87% in the group that received the higher 0.3 mg per kilogram dose following a single CRISPR-Cas9 infusion [23]. Conventional heart-failure therapy in ATTR-CA remains challenging, as these patients tolerate neurohormonal blockade poorly [9].

## Treatment of AL Amyloidosis

Therapy for AL amyloidosis targets the underlying plasma-cell clone. In the ANDROMEDA trial, daratumumab-based treatment for immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidosis was evaluated, with results published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021 [24]. The addition of subcutaneous daratumumab to bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone resulted in significantly better outcomes, establishing this quadruplet as a standard of care [24]. Outcomes nonetheless remain stage-dependent, underscoring the need for early diagnosis [6].

## Conclusion

Cardiac amyloidosis has shifted from an underrecognized, fatal condition to a treatable disease [3]. Cardiac amyloidosis is often under-recognized in its early stages, and treatments now available appear to exert their benefit predominantly in individuals with the early stages of disease [5]. Greater clinician awareness, prompt noninvasive diagnosis, and timely initiation of disease-modifying therapy are therefore essential to improving outcomes [8,14].
